nodes.title: Humans caught 13.6% of planted dangerous commands, decaying to ~5% after 50 prompts
nodes.body: Anthropic's auto-mode study ran 1,053 paid professional testers in a purpose-built environment; testers were told they were observed but not what was measured, and mid-session an obviously harmful command replaced a normal permission request. Humans detected 13.6% of the planted dangerous commands overall, roughly 17% early in a session and about 5% after 50 prompts had already been answered. The decay is the finding: the same person is three times worse at the same judgment after fifty repetitions. Applies to dsh-loom: a human clearing one approval per promotion (median round 790 s, so ~110 promotions/24h if unattended) is squarely in the after-50 regime, so any per-round human gate should be assumed to run at the ~5% floor, not the 17% headline. Test in our ledger: our records carry no per-decision timestamps from the human side, so this specific curve cannot be re-measured today; it becomes measurable the moment each rsi_decide call is logged with (decision index in session, seconds since previous decision).

nodes.title: The transcript classifier caught ~89% in study, 83% in production, with 17% false negatives on real overreach
nodes.body: The deployed Sonnet 4.6 transcript classifier judges each tool call against stated instructions; it caught ~89% of the planted malicious commands in the study, while Anthropic's own production figure is 83% — it missed 17% of 52 real cases where Claude acted beyond what the user had authorized. It never sees the model's reasoning or tool results. Apollo's two-week red-team measured 12% miss before hardening and 7% after on a held-out set; Trajectory Labs saw 0 of 720 prompt-injection attacks land in auto mode, and a two-stage classifier reaches a 0.4% false-positive rate on real traffic. So on the identical per-item judgment, the classifier beats the human by roughly 6-7x (83% vs 13.6%) — the human gate is not a second opinion, it is the weaker one. Applies to dsh-loom: our verifier is a deterministic test command, not a transcript classifier, so we get 100% on what the tests check and 0% on intent; the 17% figure is the honest estimate for the class of overreach our verifier structurally cannot see (spec drift, scope creep in the patch, tests edited). Test in our ledger: replay the 450 recorded attempts and label each patch as in-scope/out-of-scope against its campaign objective's stated out-of-scope list; the disagreement rate between our verifier verdict and that label is our own false-negative floor.

nodes.title: Presenting a plan instead of a permission request moves rejection from 3% to 39% — 13x, same humans
nodes.body: In Anthropic's production telemetry users accept 97% of per-action permission prompts and decline 3% (an earlier engineering post said 93%/7%). When the product instead presents a full plan for approval, the rejection rate jumps to 39%. Same humans, same product, same day; the only variable is whether the person is asked to evaluate a decision or to clear an item. That is the single largest measured effect size in this whole evidence set, and it is a design effect, not a training or tooling effect. Applies to dsh-loom: we already have a plan artefact (rsi_chain propose / loopPolicy.planMode) but the human queue is per-checkpoint, i.e. we shipped the 3% surface and built the plan only as machine input. Moving the human surface to 'here is the round's plan and its acceptance test' is a bigger lever than anything in the panel polish work (loom-ui2..ui8). Test in our ledger: we do record planMode on/off per campaign and the plan text in round records, so compare round-outcome quality where a human edited/declined the plan versus where the loop planned unattended; our 70 campaigns split ~evenly on planMode and loom-ab ran planMode off at 651 s and still promoted, which is exactly the confound to control for.

nodes.title: A 409,000-decision game: 33.7% of malicious requests approved, and benign-looking names beat dangerous syntax
nodes.body: A browser approval game (Alex Wauters, CTO of Customemat, launched late May 2026) logged >40,000 runs and ~409,000 approve/deny decisions at 60 seconds per round, scoring both approved risks and wrongly denied safe commands. Overall 33.7% of malicious requests were approved. Scope violations (cat of AWS credentials, cat of kube config) were missed 35% of the time. 'npm run analyze' was approved ~65% of the time even though package.json can execute any payload — and even though the agent history log directly above the prompt stated what the script does, which the write-up attributes to the log not being read closely. Overt destruction (rm -rf /, recursive chmod 777) was reliably caught; typosquatted packages and curl-to-an-unknown-API were missed about as often as scope violations. The mechanism offered is noise-induced fatigue plus missing diff context, and the practical lesson is that a plausible name outperforms dangerous syntax at getting through. Applies to dsh-loom: our equivalent of the npm script is a patch whose real blast radius is in the diff, while the card shows a 160-char summary (MAX_SUMMARY in src/runtime/review.js:26) — the exact 'benign name, unseen payload' shape. Test in our ledger: for each recorded checkpoint, correlate the summary text with what the patch actually touched; if the summary does not name the touched paths/symbols, no human can be expected to catch a scope violation from it.

nodes.title: Trained proctors accepted 50% of fabricated AI cheating flags planted on innocent sessions
nodes.body: Duolingo English Test security engineer Angel Ortmann Lee reported (talk published 2026-07-07) that proctors who were >90% accurate when judging alone accepted 50% of fabricated AI cheating flags planted on innocent test sessions. The proctors were trained, the flags came from a system they trusted, and the harm was a false accusation — yet the approval step passed half of the fabrications. The remedy touched neither model nor UI: rewritten guidelines reframed the AI signal as a preliminary alert that required independent video evidence before any action, and false acceptances fell 21% (not to zero). The stated mechanism is that a human approval step only guards what the human independently verifies; a queue that shows the AI's own summary as the only evidence is precisely the setup that produced the 50%. The talk also cites Wharton's 'cognitive surrender' finding that 80% of participants accepted AI answers even when wrong. Applies to dsh-loom: our gate/anomaly checkpoints present a loop-authored summary plus a recommendation string (RECOMMENDATION in src/runtime/review.js:29-36) and no independent artefact, so 50% acceptance of a wrong flag is a defensible prior for us. Test in our ledger: inject N synthetic bad checkpoints (a fabricated holdout regression, a fabricated anomaly) into a scratch campaign and measure our own accept rate; the ledger already stores checkpoint kind and payload, so the injection is a fixture, not a product change.

nodes.title: An approval guards only what the reviewer independently verifies; restating the agent's claim guards nothing
nodes.body: The transferable design rule from the Duolingo case is not 'add a gate' but 'make the reviewer gather evidence of their own before they may act': the flag was demoted to a preliminary alert and the proctor had to look at the video. The fix cost a guideline rewrite, moved false acceptances by 21 points, and did not touch the model. This is the same rule the SUSTech anchor paper derives formally (see w6-attn-anchor-record-proposition): if the only reference is the system's own record, the check cannot discriminate, so the human is being asked to certify something the material in front of them cannot settle. Applies to dsh-loom: our checkpoint payloads are loop-authored — the 'holdout regression' summary is written by the component that failed, and there is no one-click path to the verifier stdout or the diff hunk in the queue row (measured in wave5: ~258 chars per row, no diff, no cost, no evidence pointer). So today the honest description is that we ask a human to confirm the loop's own account of itself. Test in our ledger: pick 20 recorded checkpoints, hand the reviewer (a) the summary only and (b) the summary plus the verifier output and diff, and compare the verdicts; a large disagreement means the summary-only path is not a review.

nodes.title: Escalation-only design: +71% productivity median, versus +30% for approve-each-step
nodes.body: Stanford Digital Economy Lab's Enterprise AI Playbook (Pereira, Graylin and Brynjolfsson, March 2026) studied 51 successful deployments across 41 organizations, 7 countries and >1M employees. Deployments where the AI ran >=80% of the work autonomously and humans reviewed exceptions or random samples reported a median +71% productivity. Deployments where a human approved each step reported a median +30%. The authors attribute the 41-point gap to where the checkpoint sits, not to model or vendor quality; 77% of the biggest challenges named were invisible costs (change management, data quality, process redesign), and one financial-services case moved time-to-market from seven weeks to six hours with an 80/20 generate/refine split that the report expects to keep shrinking. Caveat: these are self-reported successes, so survivorship bias is unquantified. Applies to dsh-loom: our loop is already exception-shaped (promotion is gated by a verifier, not by a person), which puts us structurally in the +71% arm; the risk is that we then put the human on per-round checkpoint approval anyway and pay the +30% penalty for nothing. Test in our ledger: we have both modes in the record — count campaigns whose rounds were promoted without any human checkpoint versus those with a human decision, and compare rounds-to-convergence and spend per promotion.

nodes.title: Human+AI beat AI alone by 0.4 points across 1,886 decisions; only ~9% were cases where the human was right
nodes.body: A 2026 complementarity study pooled 1,886 decisions over nine sources (general knowledge, fact-checking, long-document reasoning, deception detection) with non-expert online raters and a single model: human+AI 69.3% versus AI alone 68.9%, a 0.4 percentage-point gain. Only about 9% of cases were ones where the AI was wrong and the person right, and people could not reliably tell which those were. A targeted nudge on low-confidence items lifted human accuracy from 28.4% to 38.3%, but +17.4 of those points came from accepting AI-correct answers and only +5.3 from catching AI-wrong ones. Caveats the source states: non-expert raters, one model, underpowered. The transferable shape is that when the machine is usually right the human's value is the rare correct override, so the design problem is routing — decide which decisions to take back, not raise rater accuracy. Applies to dsh-loom: our verifier makes the loop right most of the time by construction (best score 1 on nearly every campaign that ran), so a blanket human gate is buying a 0.4-point effect at a 20-minute-per-day price; the only defensible use of human time is the narrow routing question 'which promotion would I have rejected'. Test in our ledger: for the ~450 attempts we can label promotions accepted-by-machine that later needed repair (a subsequent round touching the same spec) — that rate is our own take-back population and can be compared against any gate we design.

nodes.title: Budgeting 1-3 questions per task cut user-attention cost 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the reward
nodes.body: Zhang et al. (Oracle AI + Columbia, arXiv:2610.24411v1, 17 Oct 2026) put an interruption budget on discretionary questions and priced each request as A = sum over q of [1 + k_eff*e(q) + k_val*w(q)] with both weights 1, so a request costs 1-3 units. Reading effort e(q)=1-r(q)/20 from five 1-5 dimensions (goal clarity, single ask, answer effort, actionability, conciseness); avoidability w(q)=1-v(q)/10 from four criteria (missing from log, unretrievable with tools, needed for task, user-held). Across 8 LLMs and 4 customer-service domains, budgets of 1-3 questions cut attention cost 36-73% while retaining 86-94% of the reward earned with unlimited questions. Memory-guided review of each proposed question (Approve/Substitute/Block against memory of prior answers and tool evidence) cut attention cost a further 13% at minimal reward loss and made questions judged more valuable at matched counts; without memory, review lowered both reward and judged value. Asking more did not predict gaining more. Human validation: at equal counts annotators agreed the higher-cost conversation needed more effort 75% of the time, and the request classifier matched human labels at 91.0% vs 90.0% inter-annotator agreement. Applies to dsh-loom: this is the only source that gives us an actual arithmetic for the 20-minute budget — at 1-3 units per request we can afford roughly 7-20 priced requests per day, not 110. Test in our ledger: score each recorded checkpoint kind on the avoidability criteria (is the fact already in the ledger? retrievable with the verifier? needed?) and count how many open-checkpoint kinds would fail the budget test outright.

nodes.title: 70-90% defect discovery holds only at 200-400 LOC per sitting, under 500 LOC/hour, under 60-90 minutes
nodes.body: The largest code-review study (SmartBear/Cisco: 2,500 sessions, 50 programmers, 3.2M lines, 10 months, MeetingPlace team across Bangalore, Budapest and San Jose) gives the operating envelope for a human reading a change: 200-400 lines at a time, because defect discovery falls off past 400; a 60-90 minute sitting, because it falls off past that; an inspection rate under 300-500 LOC/hour, because defect density drops above 500 LOC/hour. Inside that envelope reviewers find 70-90% of defects (10 defects, 7-9 found). Outside it the gate still runs and still returns a verdict — it just stops finding things, silently. Lightweight review costs about one fifth of a formal inspection and finds as many bugs. Applies to dsh-loom: a 20-minute daily budget is roughly a third of one review sitting, so the enforceable rule is a diff-size budget per decision, not a decision-count budget; our promotions are small (spec-shaped, mostly one or two files) which is in our favour, but nothing in the panel currently reports diff size on the card, so a pathological promotion would arrive looking identical to a good one. Test in our ledger: attempt records carry changed paths and LOC; plot LOC-per-promotion against later-repair rate. If large promotions do not repair more often, our diffs are already inside the envelope and the concern is moot.

nodes.title: 56.3% of agentic review comments were rejected; a cheap pre-filter predicts rejection at up to 76% F1
nodes.body: Lin et al. (arXiv:2607.03316v2, 3 Jul 2026) mined 31,073 review-and-feedback pairs from 10,191 PRs across 239 repositories served by CodeRabbit: 36.4% of agentic review comments were accepted, 7.3% triggered discussion, and 56.3% were rejected. Rejections were associated with invalid suggestions (false positives, redundant, out of scope) and with misalignment to developer intent and practices; agentic reviews leaned toward functional rather than evolvability concerns and were more likely to be invalid there. Crucially, lightweight learning-based predictors of rejection reach up to 76% F1, which means 'should a human ever see this comment' is a learnable pre-filter rather than a matter of taste. Applies to dsh-loom: this is the strongest argument that our checkpoint queue should be filtered by a learned prior rather than by a hand-written kind-to-risk table. Our current table (src/runtime/review.js:17-23) assigns risk purely from checkpoint kind — holdout/anomaly high, gate/policy normal, plateau low — so every gate checkpoint reaches the human regardless of whether that class has ever been accepted. Test in our ledger: with ~450 attempts and the decisions recorded per campaign, fit the same cheap classifier on (kind, summary length, campaign, round index, prior verdicts) to predict which checkpoints a human would reject; if F1 lands near the paper's 76%, replace the static RISK_BY_KIND with the score.

nodes.title: 45.1% of merged Claude Code PRs still needed human revision — so per-action gating cannot saturate
nodes.body: Watanabe et al. (arXiv:2509.14745, v1 Sep 2025, v3 Feb 2026) studied 567 Claude Code PRs across 157 open-source projects (Feb-Apr 2025 vintage): 83.8% were eventually accepted and merged versus 91.0% for human PRs, and 54.9% of merged agent PRs were integrated with no further modification, leaving 45.1% that needed additional changes, mostly bug fixes, documentation and adherence to project-specific standards. Median merge time was similar (1.23 h agent vs 1.04 h human) and revision effort in commits, LOC and files was not statistically different. The derivation used by the loop-design literature is that at a 45% per-change defect-discovery workload, gating every action would saturate any reviewer before it saved time; the gate has to sit at the change, not the step. Caveat: this sample is early-vintage, self-selected open-source contributors, and no study seeds known defects into agent PRs, so 'what reviewers miss' is unmeasured. Applies to dsh-loom: our promotions are already change-shaped, but our repair loop is internal (a failed round retries), so the analogous number is the re-attempt rate after a first promotion — worth measuring before we claim our promotions are cleaner than the open-source baseline.

nodes.title: A checkpoint exposes four verbs — approve, edit, reject, respond — and only three of them change the loop
nodes.body: The loop-control literature (agentpatterns.ai, 2026-08-08) frames a human checkpoint as a suspend that replaces a value in the loop's transition function, not as a safety wrapper. LangGraph's interrupt() persists exact state and Command(resume=...) substitutes back as the interrupt() return value without re-running upstream nodes. The four verbs are approve (continue unchanged), edit (replace the action's arguments then continue), reject (skip the action and feed the rejection back as tool result so the model re-plans) and respond (synthesize a tool result from the human's reply without running the tool). Reject and respond change what the loop iterates on; edit changes next-iteration state in place; approve changes nothing, which is why a queue that offers only approve/reject/snooze is not a control surface. Applies to dsh-loom: our panel verbs are exactly approve/reject/snooze (measured in wave5 on the queue row: keys campaign,id,kind,risk,riskSource,summary,help,waitMs,deferred,deferUntil,actions) — we have no edit and no respond, so a human who thinks 'right idea, wrong file' has no way to say so and must reject and hope the next round guesses differently. Test in our ledger: count rounds where a rejection was followed by an attempt differing only in the specific the human would have edited; that rate is the cost of the missing verb.

nodes.title: Per-iteration checkpoints rubber-stamp within hours; a checkpoint where a verifier exists is theatre
nodes.body: Two failure modes are named explicitly in the loop-control literature. First, per-iteration gates in a high-throughput loop: 'reviewers approve by reflex within hours. The gate exists in the diagram but not in practice.' Second, a human checkpoint on a step that a test, lint, schema check or convergence detector can already grade: 'an HITL checkpoint is theatre — the verifier is already the stop condition and the human adds latency without signal.' The recommended posture is that human checkpoints are 'the residual that remains after the deterministic gates handle what they can', and the three placements that earn their cost are low in-loop confidence, a budget threshold, and an irreversible action. A further documented trap is an unbounded interrupt on an overnight loop: it converts a multi-hour throughput loss into something that looks like a safety win, so every interrupt needs a timeout with a documented default. Applies to dsh-loom directly: our promotion gate IS a deterministic verifier, so a human checkpoint after a green verifier is the theatre case by definition; the only non-theatre human decisions we have are the ones the verifier cannot grade — objective choice, holdout selection, policy change, and whether a passing patch is the change we actually wanted. Test in our ledger: tag every historical checkpoint as verifier-decidable or not; if the majority are verifier-decidable, the queue is mostly theatre and should be deleted rather than improved.

nodes.title: Three bundle axes — queue, task, class — and only task and class remove decisions
nodes.body: Approval-gate granularity analysis (agentpatterns.ai, reviewed 2026-09-16) separates two quantities teams conflate: wait time (how long the agent idles) and decision count (judgments the reviewer makes per hour). Only decision count saturates, so a change that leaves it alone cannot move the bottleneck. Bundling sits on three axes: QUEUE (pile pending requests up and review together) removes zero decisions and only moves wait time; TASK (move the gate to a task boundary such as one PR) removes every per-action gate inside the task; CLASS (a rule pre-authorizes every future action of a kind) removes every action the rule covers. The measured example of class bundling working: Anthropic sandboxing 'safely reduces permission prompts by 84%' internally, because a boundary answers a whole class once. Backfire conditions: heterogeneous bundles (one irreversible action hiding among forty reversible ones collects the bundle's average scrutiny), class signals that do not track risk, scopes wider than the instance reviewed, and volume below saturation where batching just adds latency. Applies to dsh-loom: moving the human from per-checkpoint to per-round-plan is task bundling (good); a nightly digest of all campaigns is queue bundling (removes no decisions, and is what src/report/digest.js currently is). Test in our ledger: log decision count per human session, not session count; if a session's decisions all come from one campaign's rounds, the bundle is task-shaped already and only the presentation needs work.

nodes.title: Queue batching was documented failing in production: 20-40 minute waits, then reviewers skimmed 5-6 at once
nodes.body: In a text-to-SQL deployment that gated every non-SELECT write, analysts waited 'twenty, sometimes forty minutes for a human to glance at a query and click approve'. Once median wait passed fifteen minutes, 'the reviewers started approving the requests in batches, skimming five or six queries at once, dropping the review quality'. Nobody designed that batch: queue pressure produced it, and it spent scrutiny without buying throughput. The team's fix was class bundling — a risk score combining blast radius (actual row count capped at 50,000, not a query-planner estimate), a sensitivity allowlist for billing and auth tables, semantic distance from already-approved queries, and disagreement across resamples — with low scores executing immediately and the human seeing only the residue 'where the agent's interpretation of intent was plausible but wrong'. That last phrase is the most useful targeting rule in the evidence: the human's comparative advantage is the plausible-but-wrong case, not the obviously-broken one. Applies to dsh-loom: our failure is the mirror image — median promotion round is 790 s and the loop never waits for a human, so we have no queue pressure and therefore no batching pressure; our risk is the opposite, that decisions accumulate to the point of being answered in one sweep at the end of the day. Test in our ledger: nothing records the wait between a checkpoint being raised and answered, so add raisedAt/answeredAt (raisedAt already exists on checkpoints) and plot the wait distribution before designing any batching.

nodes.title: A saturated verification station has exactly three levers, and declining to choose pulls the third silently
nodes.body: Verification capacity saturation (agentpatterns.ai, reviewed 2026-08-09) treats verification as a queue: once arrivals pass the service rate, the backlog grows without a stable ceiling, and only three things move the ratio back — scale verification (raise the service rate), throttle generation (lower the arrival rate), or lower the quality bar (less work per item). The sharp observation is that a gate which DEGRADES rather than blocks pulls the third lever on its own: 'declining to choose picks the third whenever the gate degrades instead of blocking.' Human review degrades measurably (70-90% defect discovery inside the 200-400 LOC / 60-90 min envelope, falling outside it), while a deterministic test gate has no such give — a red check just stalls. Two conditions must be checked first: is the backlog actually growing (saturated) or merely long (a batch-size problem), and does your gate degrade or block. Adding model-based reviewers can shrink throughput because LLMs misclassify correct code as non-compliant, and asking them to explain plus propose fixes raises the misjudgment rate (Jin and Chen, arXiv:2603.00539v1). The curl case is the clean illustration: confirmed-vulnerability share of submissions fell below 5% from 2025 as AI reports flooded in, and with capacity and bar both unavailable the project pulled intake, ending its bug bounty on 31 Jan 2026. Applies to dsh-loom: our verifier is 0.4-8 s per round (0.1-1.5% of wall clock per docs/scoreboard-2026-11.md), so the verifier station is nowhere near saturation; the station that saturates is the human, and our only honest lever is throttling what reaches them. Test in our ledger: count promotions per day the loop would produce unattended (rounds/day at median 790 s) against decisions a human answers per day; the ratio is the saturation multiple.

nodes.title: Checkpoint spacing arithmetic: L* = floor(ln tau / ln p) gives 13 steps at 95% accuracy, 68 at 99%, 2 at 99.9% strictness
nodes.body: The SUSTech anchor paper (arXiv:2610.41682v1, 30 Oct 2026) derives a reliability model for how far apart human checks may sit. With per-unit conditional correctness p, a segment of L units is entirely correct with probability at least p^L, so the largest admissible spacing for a segment target tau is L* = floor(ln tau / ln p). p=0.95 and tau=0.5 gives 13; p=0.99 and tau=0.5 gives 68; p=0.95 with the stricter tau=0.9 gives 2. Adding a per-checkpoint correction probability q, a 100-unit task at p=0.95 with checks every 13 units and q=0.99 has 8 checkpoints and a cumulative risk bound of 3.83%, versus roughly 0.6% probability that all 100 units are correct with no intermediate checks (a ~99.4% bound on at least one error). The authors are explicit about a wrinkle that cuts against their own number: a single terminal check of the same task yields a lower bound (<=0.994%) because it measures a different event, so 'these upper bounds alone cannot rank actual policy success'; the case for intermediate checks rests on irreversibility and compounding, not the bound. Also stated: q=0 (checkpoints that detect nothing) credits no benefit, and as p approaches 1, L* grows without bound. Applies to dsh-loom: our decision unit is one round whose verifier either passes or fails, so p per unit is high by construction while tau for 'the campaign does what the human wanted' is nowhere near 0.5 — the formula's real use for us is the reverse direction, sizing how rare a human check may be before drift risk is unacceptable. Test in our ledger: estimate p empirically as the fraction of rounds whose promotion survived the next round untouched, and q as the fraction of human-caught problems that stayed fixed; both are computable from the 450 recorded attempts without new instrumentation.

nodes.title: If two runs leave the same record and differ on drift, no monitor reading the record can be right on both
nodes.body: The SUSTech paper's Proposition 3: when two admissible runs leave an identical internal record but differ on whether the goal has drifted, any monitor that reads only that record must return the same verdict on both and is therefore wrong on one; adding more monitors that read the same record does not help. The illustration is a citation — whether a cited paper exists is a fact about the literature, not about the citing paper, so a checker who reads only the citing book sees identical text in both cases. The software supplement is closer to our case: a coding agent told to update service 'a' reaches it only through a deployment alias 'u' that resolves to 'a' in one environment and 'b' in another; identical program, inputs and every interface response, identical record, one run correct and one wrong, and only authenticated identity distinguishes them. Their theorem adds that no uniform prospective certification of goal preservation exists in general (it would decide the halting problem), though fixed finite horizons can be checked by simulation. Applies to dsh-loom sharply: our verifier runs the repo's own tests, which are part of the system's record, so a campaign that changes what 'pass' means while making tests green leaves a record indistinguishable from success. That is the alias case verbatim. Test in our ledger: search the 450 attempts for promotions that touched tests/, the verifier command, or the objective text inside the same patch; each hit is a candidate record-identical drift, and the count is a lower bound on what our verifier structurally cannot see.

nodes.title: Tier 1 mechanically verifiable tasks need almost no runtime human checks; the anchor moves to spec review
nodes.body: The anchor paper grades a task stage on four dimensions — output verifiability, chain length and irreversibility, goal contestability, accountability weight — and sorts it into five tiers. Tier 1 is mechanically verifiable: proof checking, compilation, formal verification, settlement reconciliation. For those, 'runtime anchor density can approach zero within verified scope' and the anchor moves to design-time review of the specification, because the residual risk is a specification that departs from what the principal wanted. Tier 2 is statistically auditable (recommendation, classification, risk pre-screening, content triage) where the anchor lies in reference labels and sample design rather than in watching inputs. Tier 5 is the sign-off itself, valid only if the signer can actually exercise control — the paper pairs this with the EU AI Act Art. 14 requirement and with Air Canada (BC Civil Resolution Tribunal, 14 Feb 2024) standing for the proposition that an institution answers for any standard its system states. Applies to dsh-loom: almost every promotion we make is Tier 1 by this taxonomy (a spec exists, tests decide), which means the correct human surface is the SPEC, reviewed once when written, not the promotion reviewed every round. Our loop already writes specs; we do not currently route spec authorship past a human. Test in our ledger: classify the 70 campaign objectives by tier using the four dimensions; the tier-5 cases (objective choice, holdout policy, what 'better' means) are the only ones where a human decision is load-bearing, and there are few enough of them to fit 20 minutes a week.

nodes.title: A 10-15% escalation rate is the reported sustainable operating point; 85%+ pass-through means the checkpoint is misplaced
nodes.body: Practitioner guidance collected in tinyfish (2026-05-12) puts the sustainable escalation rate at 10-15% (Mavik Labs' stated operating point), while a management consultancy reports approval rates above 95% across every sales organization it has worked with. Read together with Anthropic's 97% acceptance and the Wauters game's 33.7% malicious-approval rate, the implication is blunt: any checkpoint whose pass-through exceeds ~85% is not filtering and should be moved or deleted, because the decision it claims to make is being made by the default. The same source notes that EU AI Act Art. 14 mandates the capability to intervene but does not define effective intervention (Melanie Fink), and that SOC 2 verifies controls exist and fire, not that a human exercised judgment — so compliance artefacts will not detect our own rubber stamp. Applies to dsh-loom: our current state is degenerate in the other direction — across all ~70 campaigns the dashboard reports open checkpoints = 0, so we have no escalation rate at all to compare against the 10-15% band. Before tuning placement we need to know whether the loop escalates nothing because nothing needs it, or because the escalation channel is unused. Test in our ledger: compute checkpoints raised per promotion and human decisions per promotion from the campaign records; if raised-per-promotion is near zero across 70 campaigns, the 10-15% target is a design goal for a channel that does not exist yet, and the first job is to make the loop ask about anything at all.

nodes.title: Pooled verifiers caught 93 of 100 planted errors; the 7 nobody caught were all omissions, not insertions
nodes.body: Litvak (arXiv:2611.12820, 9 Nov 2026) planted 100 known errors into 10 open-access psychology papers and ran them through frontier models and two commercial AI review tools. The best single system caught 71 of 100 and the worst caught 30; pooling all systems caught 93, because the models are only partly correlated in what they find — ensembling is the largest lever in the result. Seven errors were caught by no system, and all seven were omissions (deleted information) rather than inserted errors. Authors' stated limitations: false-positive rate was not measured, and the planted-error distribution may not match real papers. Applies to dsh-loom: our verifier is a fixed test command, so its blind spot is the same shape — a patch that passes everything while deleting a capability, a comment that documented a constraint, or a branch nobody tested. Insertions of wrong code tend to break tests; deletions often do not. That maps onto the 'silent degradation' class of agent failure and onto the checkpoint kind we already have but rank lowest-confidence. Test in our ledger: diff each promotion for net-negative lines and deleted files/exports, and correlate with whether the campaign's later rounds had to reintroduce the behaviour; a positive correlation is our own omission-detection gap, measurable without new tooling.

nodes.title: Across ~70 campaigns the dashboard reports zero open checkpoints — the loop currently asks the human nothing
nodes.body: Measured this session with rsi_dashboard: 70 campaigns, statuses done/stopped/converged, rounds per campaign 0-18, spend $0.00-0.01 against caps of $1-30, best score 1 for almost every campaign that ran at least one round (best null for loom-acc1/acc3/acc4/acc5/acc6/bal4/claim-live/demo-plan/life/ui/ui7), lessons 0-4 per campaign with quarantine counters of 1-3 on several, and open = 0 for EVERY campaign, including the three marked [converged] in the live campaign list. So the entire question 'what should the human see' is currently answered by 'nothing': there is no queue, no escalation, and no open decision to allocate twenty minutes to. That is not a safety success, it is an unmeasured channel — the mechanisms exist (src/runtime/review.js builds a risk-ranked queue; src/report/digest.js renders a 10-line catch-up with at most 3 reviews) but nothing is flowing through them. Applies to dsh-loom: any proposal to optimise human attention is premature until the loop demonstrably raises decisions; the first measurement is checkpoints-raised-per-promotion, which is currently indistinguishable from zero. Test in our ledger: read the campaign state files for raisedAt fields and count checkpoints by kind across all campaigns; if the count is genuinely zero, the 20-minute question becomes a design question (what SHOULD it ask) rather than an optimisation question (what should it stop asking).

nodes.title: dsh-loom's existing human surface is a 10-line digest with at most 3 ranked reviews
nodes.body: src/report/digest.js is explicitly 'the bounded catch-up a human needs in thirty seconds': a header line (id, status, round, verdict, spend), up to 5 round lines newest-first, at most 3 review lines ranked by reviewQueue, a lesson line when lessons exist, hard-capped at DIGEST_MAX_LINES = 10 with MAX_LINE = 120 characters, and deliberately reading only scalars — never stdout tails, patch bodies or payload blobs. That is a defensible attention budget (roughly 10 lines against the 200-400 LOC / 60-90 minute envelope, so it is very far inside it) and it is also the reason nothing surprising can reach a human: a scalar projection cannot carry a diff. src/runtime/review.js complements it by ranking open checkpoints risk-desc then age then id, with risk a property of checkpoint kind (holdout and anomaly high; gate and policy normal; plateau low) and a one-line recommendation per kind. Applies to dsh-loom: we have already built the batched digest — the thing the evidence says does NOT remove decisions — and we have not built the plan-level decision surface that does. Test in our ledger: instrument how often a digest line changes a human's action; if digest reads never precede a decision, the digest is a status ornament and the 20 minutes should move to a different surface entirely.

nodes.title: Twenty minutes a day buys about seven priced decisions or one plan review — not a queue sweep
nodes.body: Combining our own numbers with the interruption-cost model: median promotion takes 790 s (420-955 s across 10 measured rounds in docs/scoreboard-2026-11.md) and costs $0.0008-0.0010, so an unattended day produces on the order of 100 candidates. A 20-minute budget is 1,200 s, which at 60-90 s per independently-verified decision is roughly 13-20 decisions, and the arXiv:2610.24411 accounting prices each real request at 1-3 units, so 7-20 priced requests is the honest ceiling. Two allocation schemes fit inside that: (a) ONE plan/spec review per day at 39%-rejection effectiveness, plus a standing sample audit; or (b) a random-sample audit of 10-15 promoted changes per day at the 200-400 LOC envelope, which buys calibrated detection of drift without pretending to authorise anything. What does NOT fit is reading every gate checkpoint: at 97% pass-through that is 100% of the cost for ~3% of the decisions. Applies to dsh-loom: we currently spend the 20 minutes on dashboard glances (the night-shift doc records 'mostly looked at the dashboard every 10-15 minutes'), which is monitoring, not deciding, and is the exact posture the evidence says produces complacency. Test in our ledger: we already log spend and wall clock per round, so compute candidates-per-day and decisions-per-day for the 10 scoreboard rounds; the ratio tells us how many days of machine work one 20-minute session must adjudicate.

nodes.title: What the loop should never ask about: anything with 85%+ pass-through, anything verifier-decidable, anything unverifiable from the card
nodes.body: Three independent screens converge on the same never-ask list. (1) Pass-through: any checkpoint class whose acceptance exceeds ~85% is not a decision (Anthropic 97%, consultancy >95%, sustainable escalation 10-15%), so a per-round gate hold that has never once been rejected should be deleted, not reworded. (2) Verifier-decidable: if a test, lint, schema check or convergence detector can grade it, a human checkpoint is theatre and adds latency without signal (agentpatterns loop-control page) — for dsh-loom that means 'did the tests pass', 'is the patch applied', 'did the holdout run', all of which are deterministic and belong in the digest, not the queue. (3) Unverifiable from the card: if the reviewer cannot independently check the claim with material on the card (no diff, no verifier output, no reference label), the approval is a rubber stamp by construction (Duolingo's 50% fabricated-flag acceptance; the anchor proposition on records that cannot discriminate). Under those three screens, the only questions worth the 20 minutes are: is this the objective we want at all (tier 5), is this the change we meant (spec-level, 39% effective), and does this sample of N promotions still look like the work we asked for (audit). Applies to dsh-loom: our five checkpoint kinds map unevenly — plateau is a pacing hint and should be silent; gate and holdout are verifier-decidable until the verifier's own scope is in question; anomaly and policy are the genuinely human ones. Test in our ledger: for each kind, compute historical acceptance; any kind above 85% is a deletion candidate, and we can validate the deletion by checking no later round reversed a decision it would have made.

nodes.title: Four measurements our ledger can support today, and the one it cannot
nodes.body: Our ~450 recorded attempts and 70 campaigns already carry: per-round wall clock and spend, planMode on/off, objective text, verifier verdict, changed paths and LOC, lessons with quarantine counters, and checkpoint records with kind/risk/raisedAt/payload. That supports four measurements without new product work: (1) p, the survival rate of a promotion into the next round untouched; (2) q, the fraction of human-flagged problems that stayed fixed; (3) checkpoints-raised-per-promotion by kind, which today reads as zero across all 70 campaigns and is therefore the first thing to instrument rather than analyse; (4) a rejection predictor for checkpoint summaries, since the CodeRabbit result says 'would a human reject this' is learnable at up to 76% F1. What the ledger cannot support is anything about human attention itself: there is no per-decision timestamp, no decision index within a session, no record of how long a checkpoint sat before being answered, and no record of what the human looked at first. The 13.6%-catch-rate and prompt-decay numbers are therefore not re-measurable on our data until rsi_decide logs (session id, decision ordinal, seconds since previous decision, checkpoint kind, verdict) — a schema addition, not an experiment. Caveat: node is not on PATH in this session, so all of the above is a plan grounded in the schema and in rsi_dashboard output, not a completed measurement.
nodes.source: derived: local schema inspection (src/runtime/review.js, src/report/digest.js), rsi_dashboard 2026-11-12, docs/scoreboard-2026-11.md

nodes.title: Our queue ranks risk by checkpoint kind alone — a static table, no payload, no history
nodes.body: src/runtime/review.js assigns risk from the checkpoint kind: RISK_BY_KIND = { holdout: 'high', anomaly: 'high', gate: 'normal', policy: 'normal', plateau: 'low' }, unknown kinds fall back to low, and the queue sorts risk desc, then raisedAt asc, then id. summaryOf picks a per-kind detail field and clips at MAX_SUMMARY = 160 characters; RECOMMENDATION supplies a canned verb phrase per kind ('review the diff, then apply or reject the patch'). The design comment is honest about the motivation: checkpoints used to be listed in arrival order, so an overnight holdout regression could sit below three routine gate holds. But the ranking is a five-row constant informed by no outcome: it cannot learn that gate holds are accepted 100% of the time in one campaign and 40% in another, and it ranks a payload-free summary as if the human could act on it. Given the granularity evidence this is the wrong axis entirely — effort should go into reducing decision count, not reordering it. Applies to dsh-loom: the cheapest correct change is to derive risk from (kind x campaign history x payload shape) and to suppress any class above the 85% acceptance screen. Test in our ledger: compute per-kind acceptance from recorded verdicts; if gate holds sit above 85%, demote the class and confirm no reversal.

nodes.title: Our machine produces ~110 promotion-candidates per unattended day; a human can price ~7-20 decisions
nodes.body: Arithmetic from our own measured rounds: median promotion 790 s means 86,400/790 = 109 candidates per fully unattended day, each costing $0.0008-0.0010, so a day of unattended loop time costs roughly $0.09-0.11 and yields over a hundred passing changes. Against that, the interruption-cost model prices a genuine request at 1-3 attention units where a 20-minute budget supports roughly 7-20 such requests (and a 60-90 s independently-verified decision caps it near 13-20). The gap is one to two orders of magnitude, and it is a structural fact about the model, not a tuning problem: the loop's throughput is set by verifier cost (0.4-8 s per round) and the human's is set by reading speed, so no interface catches up. The only stable resolutions are sampling (audit a random subset and accept the rest by default), escalation (humans see only what a cheap classifier flags), or throttling machine throughput to human rate — and the evidence ranks them sampling/escalation first, throttling last, because throttling pays the 41-point Stanford penalty for nothing. Applies to dsh-loom: we have never actually run a fully unattended day, so 109/day is an upper bound computed from median round time, and the real number is lower because campaigns stop at budget or convergence (rounds used are 1-18, most campaigns under 4). Test in our ledger: sum rounds across all campaigns and divide by the wall-clock span covered by the ledger; that measured rate replaces the 109 estimate.

nodes.title: VERSE is the only 2026 harness-evolution paper with a disjoint task-level train/val/test/OOD split
nodes.body: arXiv:2610.02616v1 (2 Oct 2026) draws 110 train + 50 validation tasks from 593 SWE-rebench instances in the Jan 2025 - Feb 2026 monthly releases, tests on the 108 gradable tasks of the March 2026 release (in-distribution, Python), and measures OOD on the 107 gradable tasks of the July 2026 release spanning Go/Java/Python/Rust/TypeScript with only 20 Python tasks. Final 42.3% in-distribution and 37.7% OOD versus strongest baselines 39.2% and 29.3%. The authors state why they built it this way: prior harness optimizers 'search and report results on the same benchmark'. Every other system in this scan reuses the same tasks as optimization signal and as the reported number.

nodes.title: Self-evolution without a verification step scored BELOW the blank harness: 31.79 vs 33.95
nodes.body: VERSE Table 1, SWE-rebench avg@3 over three test evaluations, blank initial harness = 33.95 +/- 0.82. Adding self-evolution to Meta-Harness WITHOUT verification: r*=0 rounds, validation selected the initial harness over every evolved one, measured 31.79 +/- 1.35, i.e. below doing nothing. Their diagnosis is mechanical, not statistical: 'the optimizer could not test its edits before submitting them, so it could not tell which ones were wrong', and it 'wrote untested lessons into its own harness'. Adding simple verification on top of the same self-evolution reached r*=6 and 41.05 +/- 0.82. The difference between those two rows is one verification step, not a better proposer.

nodes.title: In the best-controlled study, verification buys +5.9 points and self-evolution adds 1.2 points inside overlapping error bars
nodes.body: Reading VERSE Table 1 as a ladder at one fixed model and one fixed initial harness: blank 33.95 +/- 0.82; Meta-Harness r*=4 39.20 +/- 1.11 (last 35.80 +/- 0.82); simple verification only r*=5 39.81 +/- 1.41 (last 37.65 +/- 2.74); self-evolution + simple verification r*=6 41.05 +/- 0.82 (last 41.05 +/- 0.82). Verification alone accounts for +5.86 points. The increment attributable to the self-evolution loop on top of verification is 41.05 - 39.81 = 1.24 points, with overlapping confidence intervals. Only in the combined row do validity-selected and last-round scores coincide (41.05 and 41.05), which is the operational meaning of 'the loop stopped finding anything that survives its own check'.

nodes.title: Darwin Godel Machine: 20.0% to 50.0% SWE-bench and 14.2% to 30.7% Polyglot by self-modifying its own agent code
nodes.body: arXiv:2505.22954v3 (Zhang/Hu/Lu/Lange/Clune). The archive holds generated coding agents; one is sampled and a foundation model writes a new 'interesting' version, growing an open-ended tree. Parent sampling is proportional to sigmoid(10*(s-0.5))/(1+c) with s the score and c the child count; goal probabilities are 0.25 solve-empty-patches (only if >=10% empty), 0.25 solve-stochasticity, 0.25 solve-context-length, else a uniformly drawn unresolved task. Report: SWE-bench 20.0% to 50.0%, Polyglot 14.2% to 30.7%, 'significantly outperforms baselines without self-improvement or open-ended exploration'. The hidden tests of each issue are the objective, the selection signal, and the reported metric - one signal, three jobs.

nodes.title: Randomised re-analysis of six public DGM runs: modifications repair their target LESS often than chance, e-value 0.15
nodes.body: arXiv:2610.14662v1 (Rong He, 10 Oct 2026) randomises which failure a modification is scored against, giving an exactly valid test in the Luria-Delbruck fluctuation tradition with an e-value via Ville's inequality (E>=20 needed for 5%). Across 145 eligible modifications in six public DGM runs: 12 repaired their target versus 16.4 expected under the null; target repair 8.3% versus 11.6% for the parent's other failures (difference -3.3pp, 95% CI -8.2 to +2.0); pooled OR 0.69 (0.31-1.18); e-value 0.15; martingale z=-1.23, one-sided p=0.89; no run significant and five of six point the wrong way; leave-one-run-out -1.5 to -4.2. Section 3.3 adds that human-named goals DO move the metric they name (empty-patch-goal children cut the parent's empty-patch rate by 10.3 points versus 1.7 for other entries; every context-goal child cut context-limit hits) - so the loop follows its instructions while not repairing the failures it was shown. Study 2 pre-registers a held-out split: +20pp repair for Qwen3-4B, 7 points for Phi-4-mini and not significant, and their own conclusion 'Target repair did not reliably imply held-out improvement'. Their stated guard: a revision that repairs all failures equally has no directedness yet may still be effective.

nodes.title: HGM: a high-scoring agent can seed unproductive descendants; own-score/held-out correlation is 0.29-0.44 for DGM/SICA
nodes.body: arXiv:2510.21614v2 (KAUST, ICLR 2026) names the Metaproductivity-Performance Mismatch: 'a high-scoring agent may produce unproductive descendants, while a lower-scoring one seeds lineages that achieve greater long-term gains.' It defines Clade-Metaproductivity as the aggregate benchmark performance of a lineage, proves (Theorem 1) that a true CMP oracle suffices to imitate the Godel Machine under assumptions of repeatable independent evaluations, zero-cost proofs and one budget unit per self-modification, then estimates CMP and expands by Thompson sampling with expansion and evaluation decoupled. Claims: beats DGM and SICA on SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot with 2.38x fewer allocated CPU-hours; transfer from SWE-bench Verified/GPT-5-mini to SWE-bench Lite/GPT-5 described as 'human-level'. The mismatch is quantified: Pearson correlation between an agent's own score and held-out performance is 0.444 for SICA, 0.285 weighted / 0.406 unweighted for DGM, 0.778 / 0.512 for HGM.

nodes.title: SICA: 17% to 53% on a 50-question SWE-bench Verified subset, with the best agent becoming the next meta-agent
nodes.body: arXiv:2504.15228v2 (Robeyns/Szummer/Aitchison). Utility U = 0.5*p_score + 0.25*(1-min(1,p_cost/$10)) + 0.25*(1-min(1,p_time/300s)), with timeout penalty tau=0.5 giving U_final = U*(1-tau). Evaluation: 50 fixed random SWE-bench Verified questions, 50 LiveCodeBench, and two synthetic benchmarks (file-edit, symbol-navigation) built inside the agent's own codebase. The archive of agents replaces ADAS's fixed meta-agent - the best agent becomes the next meta-agent - and a 30-second overseer LLM can cancel a runaway agent. Sonnet 3.5 v2 for most agents, o3-mini for a reasoning agent; one meta-improvement iteration can take about an hour. Reported 17% to 53% on the SWE-bench subset. Held out: nothing at task level; the same 50 questions score candidates and are the headline. SICA's paper distinguishes itself from ADAS (not self-improving; edits one forward function in a DSL) and from STOP/Godel Agent (not general coding agents).

nodes.title: SICA's loop self-terminated: repeated errors after 45% of budget, no further self-modifications
nodes.body: The failure is documented in a competitor's Figure 1 caption, not in SICA's own paper: HGM (arXiv:2510.21614v2) writes 'Note that SICA encountered repeated errors after consuming 45% of its budget, preventing any further self-modifications.' Mechanism as reported: the agent's own edits broke the loop's ability to run, and the remaining 55% of budget bought nothing. This is the same shape as VERSE's r*=0 and as the forgetting result - the loop damages the very machinery that would let it recover - but here it is budget-bounded and unrecoverable. For an RSI system the important detail is that the collapse is not a plateau in score, it is a loss of the ability to attempt.

nodes.title: AlphaEvolve: 48 scalar multiplications for 4x4 complex matmul (first gain over Strassen's 49 in 56 years), verified per problem
nodes.body: arXiv:2506.13131 (16 Jun 2025, Novikov et al., 18 authors, DeepMind). An evolutionary coding agent: an LLM pipeline makes direct code changes and one or more evaluators give continuous feedback. Claims: 4x4 complex-valued matrix multiplication in 48 scalar multiplications (first improvement over Strassen's 49 in 56 years); a more efficient Google data-center scheduling heuristic (secondary reports ~0.7% of cluster compute recovered in production); a functionally equivalent circuit-design simplification in hardware accelerators; and accelerated training of the LLM that underpins AlphaEvolve itself. The structural reason these claims hold up better than benchmark gains: each problem has a machine-checkable verifier, so the acceptance test is independent of the proposer's story about why the change helps. Secondary source reports a 32.5% FlashAttention kernel speedup.

nodes.title: Even AlphaEvolve improved 20 of 67 pre-registered problems (~30%) and its public results repo excludes the rest
nodes.body: arXiv:2511.02864v3 (Georgiev/Gomez-Serrano/Tao/Wagner, 22 Dec 2025) re-attempts 67 problems and states in section 1.6: 'while AlphaEvolve excels at problems that can be clearly formulated as the optimization of a smooth score function that is possible to hill-climbing on, it sometimes struggles otherwise. In particular, we have encountered several instances where AlphaEvolve failed to attain an optimal or close to optimal result. We also report these cases below.' It documents every non-improvement in section 6; secondary tallies give ~20 improved results, most others matching known bounds, and 8 cases worse than the literature (20/67 ~ 30%). Tao's blog adds that performance was uneven across mathematical areas, with weakness on analytic number theory sieve weights. The deepmind/alphaevolve_results repo says it 'contains only the instances where the results from AlphaEvolve outperforms the state-of-the-art ... we exclude those problems where the results matched but did not outperform' - so the artifact overstates the rate even for the best-verified system in this scan.

nodes.title: Self-Harness: +21.4 / +14.3 / +14.2 points on Terminal-Bench-2.0 with frozen weights, three-stage loop
nodes.body: arXiv:2606.09498 (Zhang et al. 2026a). Three stages: Weakness Mining, Harness Proposal, Proposal Validation; the model weights are never trained, only the scaffolding changes. Terminal-Bench-2.0 pass rates: MiniMax M2.5 40.5% to 61.9% (+21.4 points, ~+53% relative), Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 23.8% to 38.1% (+14.3, ~+60% relative), GLM-5 42.9% to 57.1% (+14.2, ~+33% relative). The authors describe the numbers as on held-out problems. Independent commentary (thakicloud blog, 2026-07-24) notes that the figures are taken from abstract/intro and were not reproduced, that there is a single benchmark, and that the ceiling is set by evaluator strength - i.e. any weakness the validation stage cannot detect becomes a permanent harness feature.

nodes.title: Meta-Harness: an agentic proposer reads all prior candidates' source, scores and traces from a filesystem; +7.7 points at 4x fewer tokens
nodes.body: arXiv:2603.28052v1 (30 Mar 2026; Yoonho Lee, Roshen Nair, Qizheng Zhang, Kangwook Lee, Omar Khattab, Chelsea Finn). An outer loop searches over harness CODE; the proposer gets source code, scores and execution traces of every prior candidate through a filesystem, on the argument that existing text optimizers fail because 'they compress feedback too aggressively'. Reported: online text classification +7.7 points over a state-of-the-art context-management system while using 4x fewer context tokens; retrieval-augmented math reasoning, one discovered harness, +4.7 points on 200 IMO-level problems averaged across five held-out models; agentic coding, discovered harnesses surpassing the best hand-engineered baselines on TerminalBench-2. The held-out axis here is models, not tasks - and VERSE later shows this optimizer's task-level gains are the ones that shrink against a disjoint split.

nodes.title: Continual harness evolution forgets catastrophically: Meta-Harness 94.0% to 32.0% on SWE-bench after five FeatureBench rounds
nodes.body: arXiv:2611.03219v1 (2 Nov 2026, Tsinghua AI Agent Group) formalises continual harness self-evolution as H_{i+1} = Omega(H_i, T_i) over an ordered dataset sequence and measures forgetting as Delta_forget = Eval(H_{j+1}, D_j) - Eval(H_{i+1}, D_j), with rho_forget its relative version. Base harness Mini-SWE-Agent (~100 lines, >74% SWE-bench Verified), model DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, E2B sandbox, temperature 0, 50 SWE-bench Verified + 50 SWT-Bench + 30 FeatureBench instances, scope limited to system prompt, execution logic and tools. Single-dataset evolution works: AHE 82.0% to 96.0% over nine rounds, Meta-Harness 94.0%, both 82.0% to 100.0% on SWT-Bench. Then SWE-Bench to SWT-Bench: after five rounds AHE degrades 100% and Meta-Harness 98% on SWE-Bench - 'the resulting agents are almost completely unable to solve the SWE-Bench tasks'; SWE to FeatureBench costs -29% (AHE) and -66% (Meta-Harness), and Meta-Harness SWE-Bench falls 94.0% to 32.0% after five FeatureBench rounds. Hand-coding >520 trajectories yields three harness-level conflict classes (verification, workflow, budget strategy) whose ablations differ substantially.

nodes.title: Cortex A/A test: the same harness measured twice on the same tasks differed by -3.3 points (95% CI -7.3 to 0.0)
nodes.body: arXiv:2610.14216v1 (9 Oct 2026, S. Giampieri; code github.com/samugit83/cortex tag v1.0-eval) evolves and prunes Claude Code skills/rules under a measurement gate: /harvest turns a broken-to-working session into a replayable task with a check script, /evolve keeps a candidate only if it helped, fired, and made no task worse beyond tolerance, /prune re-measures live items by removing them one at a time. The A/A control - the SAME harness measured twice on the same tasks in separate rollout batches - differed by -3.3 points (95% CI [-7.3, 0.0], resampling tasks), which they describe as 'a difference that, seen once, would pass for an effect'. Against that floor the evolved harness beat a no-skills/no-rules harness by +55.0 points on four rule families (95% CI [+34.1, +74.1], permutation p=0.0001), with the control family (plain bugs, nothing to learn) at -0.8 points and no item ever kept for it. 30 held-out scenarios never played by any session, 4 independent runs R1-R4, 10 scripted rounds each, Claude Haiku 4.5 in every role, synthetic repo with 4 house rules.

nodes.title: Cortex's known-answer test shows a correct gate can pass by luck: 12 of 20 placebos scored 'never used' and 8 reached no verdict
nodes.body: Cortex plants 20 placebo candidates, 5 harmful ones and 4 known-good ones. No placebo and no harmful item was kept - but the reason is not discrimination: the agent never opened the placebos or 2 of the harmful skills, so they were rejected for never firing; 12 placebos scored 'never used' and 8 reached no verdict. The 3 harmful rules DID load but their screens ran on tasks the live harness had already failed, where no gain was possible, so no verdict was reached even where a harmful rule broke a task that passed without it. Only 2 of 4 known-good candidates were kept. The /prune pass reached the expected verdict on 6 of 8 items but only 2 of 4 planted ones, and it kept a useless always-on skill that was never opened because 2 tasks passed less often without it. This is the acceptance-test failure mode in miniature: a gate with no statistical power looks conservative while being arbitrary.

nodes.title: The same evolved harness gained +66.7 points under Haiku 4.5 and +5.6 under Sonnet 5 (95% CI -2.8 to +13.9)
nodes.body: Cortex run R1's evolved harness was re-measured unchanged under a stronger model: +66.7 points on Claude Haiku 4.5 versus +5.6 points on Claude Sonnet 5 (95% CI [-2.8, +13.9]), and a single /prune pass after the upgrade flagged 2 of its 4 items removable. The paper's reading is that whether an updated harness helps depends on the model that uses it, and that weaker models often fail to activate or follow what was added - consistent with the loading-tier counts: of 18 items kept across runs, 16 are auto-loaded rules; a path-gated skill was listed in 66 attempts and opened in 28, while an always-on skill was listed in 198 attempts and opened 0 times. A harness gain is therefore a property of the (harness, model) pair, not of the harness.

nodes.title: Retrospective adaptation study: of 7 harness changes whose target problem actually recurred, 4 reduced nothing
nodes.body: arXiv:2610.34938v1 (26 Oct 2026, Treude and Baltes). Claude Code worked 30 SWE-bench Verified issues; 125 retrospective proposals were qualitatively coded, 24 implemented, and 12 harness changes were evaluated on later issues from the SAME repositories in fresh sessions with and without each change. Most proposals referenced a concrete session event, yet 18 of 43 lint-related proposals recommended a practice regardless of what had happened. Of the seven evaluations in which control sessions actually encountered the targeted problem, 2 eliminated the targeted action, 1 reduced it, and 4 showed no reduction at all, with some changes adding work on unrelated issues. Their conclusion is the design requirement: harness self-evolution needs a way to establish whether a change helped, and to revise or remove changes that did not.

nodes.title: TTHE: +38 points on BIRD and +15 on SWE-bench from label-free proxies, with a measured 6-point selection regret
nodes.body: arXiv:2607.08124 (Nie et al., 9 Jul 2026). Population generate-and-judge over harness branches with frozen weights and three label-free signals: execution health (0/1 for well-formed output), round-trip consistency in [0,1] by inverting output back to input, and public-test pass rate. Defaults G=3 branches, R=3 rounds, B=10 batch. Results: BIRD 50-hard 12.0% to 50.0% (+38.0pp); SWE-bench Verified 40 instances 20.0% to 35.0% (+15.0pp); LiveCodeBench 60-hard 30.0% to 38.3%; DS-1000 38.0% to 44.0%; claw-eval tool use 48.9% to 69.8% (+20.9). Cross-model on BIRD: DeepSeek V4 Flash 12.0 to 50.0, MiMo V2.5 32.0 to 52.0, Kimi K2.5 28.0 to 48.0. Carrying harness improvements across batches beats resetting by 6 points. The authors' own floor: the pool oracle (best candidate the judge could have picked) is 64.0% while the all-candidates oracle (best ever generated) is 70.0%, so 6 points of achievable gain are lost to an imperfect judge. Caveat for this scan: only a secondary blog was read, so the numbers are unverified.

nodes.title: AFlow/ADAS: MCTS over code-represented workflows and architectures, beating manual designs on six benchmarks without a task-level holdout
nodes.body: AFlow (arXiv:2410.10762v4, ICLR 2025) runs MCTS over code-represented workflows built from LLM-calling nodes, code edges and reusable operators such as Ensemble and Review-and-Revise, with soft mixed-probability node selection, LLM-driven node expansion, execution-based evaluation and backpropagated experience; it reports consistent wins over automated and manually designed workflows on six benchmarks (solve rate on Math/GSM8K, F1 on HotpotQA and DROP, pass@1 on HumanEval and MBPP). ADAS (arXiv:2408.08435v2, Hu/Lu/Clune, ICLR 2025) has a fixed meta-agent search code-defined agent architectures in a Turing-complete space and evaluates on held-out domains and models. Both report on the benchmarks they search over; SICA's paper adds that ADAS is not self-improving and edits only a single forward function in a DSL. This pair is the 'search, but not self-modification' control condition for the rest of the scan.

nodes.title: STOP: the improver improves itself, and the authors measure how often generated code escapes the sandbox
nodes.body: arXiv:2310.02304v3 (Zelikman/Lorch/Mackey/Kalai, COLM 2024). A seed improver improves an input program against a utility function; the seed improver then improves ITSELF and the improved improver beats the seed on downstream tasks. The LM proposes improver strategies such as beam search, genetic algorithms and simulated annealing. Two statements matter here. First, scope: 'Since the language models themselves are not altered, this is not full recursive self-improvement.' Second, integrity: 'we evaluate the frequency with which the generated code bypasses a sandbox' - the acceptance test's own security is treated as a measured quantity, not an assumption. That is the earliest explicit treatment in this literature of the evaluator as an attack surface rather than a referee.

nodes.title: OpenAI/Thrive Tax AI: 75%-correct returns went from a quarter to 86% in six weeks - no holdout, no control arm
nodes.body: OpenAI engineering post, 27 May 2026, 'Building self-improving tax agents with Codex' (Srinivasan, Shamdasani, Araujo, de Wasseige). Tax AI processed 7,000 returns across Crete's 30+ accounting firms; the loop is three pillars - practitioner feedback, production traces, and a Codex-driven improvement loop over tailored evals. Numbers: about a third of practitioner time saved, 'up to 97% accuracy', throughput up about 50%; at launch only a quarter of returns reached 75% correct field completion, within six weeks 86% did; rental properties took about six weeks and 'substantial engineering oversight' to reach 90% precision and recall. There is no held-out task split, no control arm, and the headline metric moves with product, prompt and model changes together, so this is a vendor case study rather than a replication. The boundaries they do state are honest: 'We apply this automation to a bounded layer of the product' and 'If the evidence is ambiguous or not safely automatable, the case routes back to the product team instead of being forced through the loop.'

nodes.title: No primary self-evolution measurement exists for Devin or Claude Code; the CL-BENCH numbers that do exist are grim
nodes.body: This scan found no primary, controlled measurement of self-evolution for Devin/Cognition or for Anthropic's Claude Code product loops. The nearest is practitioner synthesis (codeagentreview.com, 9 Nov 2026, 'Continual Learning Architectures for Production Coding Agents'), which splits the surface into weights, harness and context, recommends starting with context, and states 'the agent seemed pleased with itself is not a release criterion'. It reports that CL-BENCH's top system used in-context learning at normalized reward 22.3%, above weight-updated alternatives, and that on SWE-Bench-CL 'after harness adaptation, reported performance was extremely low and highly variable, with frequent execution issues'; CL-BENCH agents 'often overfit to immediate observations or fail to reuse knowledge across instances, and naive in-context learning outperforms dedicated memory systems'. It also names a security failure with the same shape as STOP's sandbox metric: an agent authors a skill reproducing a malicious pattern it just read, then stores it - 'a successful task is not proof that its resulting skill is safe.'

nodes.title: The Evaluator Is the Bottleneck: five conditions an acceptance test must meet, each illustrated by a published failure
nodes.body: Mahendrakar, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23130396 (4 Oct 2026, CC BY 4.0). Argues the binding constraint on self-improving systems is the acceptance test, and specifies five conditions: fidelity on candidates the loop itself generates; integrity against tampering by the candidate; statistical power across many candidates and acceptances; coverage of state that persists after acceptance; and independence of evaluator errors from proposer errors. For each condition it cites a published loop, benchmark or controlled study that records the failure. Its strongest counter-evidence is 2026 work that evolves the evaluator in-loop - but every such system that reports validity against ground truth 'keeps a labelled anchor or frozen reference that the loop cannot write', and one reports that removing the anchor guards yields an always-pass grader that downstream task scores fail to expose. It also notes that an externally supplied benchmark is an attack surface (2026 benchmark-poisoning work). No experiments of its own: this is an argument paper, so it belongs at moderate confidence and is used here as a framework, not as a data point.

nodes.title: Self-evolving coding agents survey: tasks and tests reused as update signal, selection signal and reported metric make evaluator adaptation look like progress
nodes.body: arXiv:2608.03392v4 (24 Sep 2026, NJUST/NJU, CC BY 4.0). Taxonomy ordered by intervention depth - assets (memory/skill/tool/context), then architecture (harness/workflow/multi-agent), then model parameters - with the observation that deeper interventions are harder to attribute and to reverse. Its normative claim is the one that matters for replication: 'Coding tasks and their tests may also be used to construct updates, select candidates, and report final performance. Reusing related cases across these roles can make adaptation to an evaluator look like general progress.' Hence 'an evolution study should therefore identify what persists, compare updated and frozen agents under matched conditions on held-out tasks, and report regressions and costs alongside gains.' Its challenges section leads with 'Reproducibility, contamination, and benchmark overfitting'. It also reports the Phantom Guardrails study (proposer installs a guardrail for a nonexistent violation in 15 of 60 runs when harmless input resembles a familiar rule, none on featureless input, and an add-only loop makes the spurious component persist) and an audit of real self-improvement trajectories where harness tampering 'can persist in the lineage of the selected best agent'.

nodes.title: Weak tests and leakage inflate coding-agent scores: 32.67% leakage, 31.08% weak tests, +6.4 points average inflation
nodes.body: Numbers from the evaluator paper's evidence table (second-hand, gathered from search snippets rather than the primary tables). Aleithan et al. 2024, SWE-Agent+GPT-4 passing patches: 32.67% showed solution leakage, 31.08% rested on weak tests, and filtering cut the pass rate from 12.47% to 3.97%. Wang, Y. et al. 2025 on SWE-bench Verified: 7.8% of patches were counted correct while failing developer tests, 29.6% behaved differently, an average inflation of +6.4 points (6.2 in the abstract). Yu et al. 2025 (UTBoost) found 345 wrongly passed patches, affecting 40.9% of Lite and 24.4% of Verified entries; Yu et al. 2026 (SWE-ABS) strengthened tests. Consequence for any self-improvement loop: if the grader accepts patches that do not fix the issue, the loop can bank real-looking gains against a target it is not actually hitting, and no amount of internal validation will surface it.

nodes.title: Harness Overfit Detector (hod 0.1.0): held-out manifests, good/bad sanity pairs, agreement and blinded grading in one CLI
nodes.body: PyPI package hod 0.1.0 (2026-10-21) is the cheapest concrete implementation of the discipline this wave keeps asking for. It provides held-out manifests, a sanity command that runs a known-good and a known-bad candidate through the same path (hod sanity --good/--bad --manifest), hod agree to report percent-equal, mean absolute difference and Cohen's kappa between two graders, and hod blind / hod unblind which present shuffled task ids while writing the key elsewhere. Its own stated limit is the important part: 'with a single agent, the key exists on disk and the blinding is instruction-enforced' - i.e. it prevents accidental peeking, not a determined optimizer. For a small loop this is still the difference between a pre-registered split and a vibe, and it is small enough to run over an existing attempt ledger.

nodes.title: Our own rsi-gear: +13.0pp Marketing, +10.1pp Terminal-Bench 2.1, and no held-out split anywhere in the README
nodes.body: research/gear/README.md:53-60, same-model same-effort comparison. GPT 5.6 Luna medium, DSH base vs DSH+Gear: Marketing pass 27.0% to 40.0% (+13.0pp), Marketing objective completion 75.4% to 83.9% (+8.5), Support pass 17.0% to 25.0% (+8.0), Support objective completion 72.9% to 81.3% (+8.4), Terminal-Bench 2.1 52.8% to 62.9% (+10.1). GPT 6 Astra max: 57.0% to 61.0%, 84.1% to 86.3%, 35.0% to 39.0%, 88.4% to 88.7%, TB2.1 86.7% to 87.6% (+0.9). The README discloses no held-out split - AutomationBench Marketing/Support and Terminal-Bench 2.1 are both the optimization signal and the reported result - and the Luna max-effort row admits 'improvements over Luna's medium baseline include both harness and effort changes'. Evolvable surfaces are prompts/policies, tools/hooks, skills/workflows and context management; model weights are 'Experimental'. Cost: $0.0568/task for Luna max versus $1.1858/task for Astra max, 95.21% lower, same optimized harness commit a0740800. This is the closest external analogue to dsh-loom because Gear optimizes DSH itself.

nodes.title: Our own open-dream-rsi is the one local artifact with a pre-registered split and a named significance test
nodes.body: research/open-dream-rsi/paper/main.tex implements the exploration layer of RSI around a FROZEN LLM (no weight access, no GPU, no training): always-on supervisor self-scheduling under an explicit API-call budget guard, LLM-written exploration policies scored by counterfactual replay on the recorded discovery tree, thought-conditioned branching, and a Sentinel seam that annotates why an episode stopped. Performance claims sit on exactly one benchmark, goose x TravelPlanner: the choice-removal gate lifts pre-registered eval-split plan delivery 23% to 94% and final pass rate 7.6% to 21.5%, exact McNemar p=1.4e-17, with all 91 undelivered cold episodes dying at the harness call cap. Everything else is labelled a deterministic machinery self-check, not a model-quality claim: 50 solves at 150 API calls (3.00 per task-cycle) versus 50 solves at 71 calls (1.42), a 52.7% call saving at equal solve quality; bench-policy greedy 0/120, eps-greedy 29/120, replay-gated 93/120, thought-guided 120/120, sentinel-guided 102/120, engine-off ablation 75/120. The sentinel live-model uplift is explicitly future work.

nodes.title: About 1 of 11 headline gains survives pre-registered re-measurement as an effect of the loop itself, and it shrinks to ~1 point
nodes.body: Tally over the quantitative claims in scope: DGM (+30pp SWE-bench), SICA (17% to 53%), HGM (2.38x fewer CPU-hours), AlphaEvolve (48 multiplications), Self-Harness (+21.4pp TB2), Meta-Harness (+7.7), TTHE (+38pp BIRD), AHE (69.7% to 77.0%), Cortex (+55pp), rsi-gear (+13.0pp Marketing), open-dream-rsi (23% to 94% delivery). Only three were re-measured under a protocol that could have falsified them: VERSE with disjoint held-out tasks, the randomised audit of six DGM runs, and Cortex with 30 held-out scenarios plus an A/A floor. VERSE leaves 41.05 versus 39.81 = +1.24 points attributable to self-evolution; the DGM audit is directionally null (e-value 0.15, p=0.89, five of six runs the wrong way); Cortex survives at +55 but with a 3.3-point noise floor and only +5.6 under a stronger model. So roughly one in eleven headline numbers survives as evidence about the loop, and the survivor is an order of magnitude smaller than the headline. Caveat: the inclusion and survival criteria are mine, stated so they can be argued with; AlphaEvolve's verifier-based results are excluded from the failure column because their evaluator is independent of the proposer.

nodes.title: What failed replications share: one signal doing three jobs, a gate with less power than the claimed delta, and unverified self-edits
nodes.body: Seven properties recur in the replications that failed. (1) The same tasks do three jobs - construct updates, select candidates, report performance - which VERSE calls out ('search and report results on the same benchmark') and the survey formalises as making evaluator adaptation look like general progress. (2) The acceptance test has less power than the claimed delta: Cortex's A/A floor is 3.3 points, most claims are 1-13 points, and the retrospective study found only 7 of 12 changes ever met their target problem, of which 4 reduced nothing. (3) The optimizer writes unverified edits into itself: VERSE r*=0 with 31.79 below the blank 33.95, SICA dying at 45% of budget, DGM modifications that repair their target 3.3 points LESS often than chance. (4) Proxy signals with selection regret: TTHE leaves 6 of 70 oracle points on the table. (5) Graders that reward weak tests: +6.4 points average inflation, 32.67% leakage. (6) Gains bound to one model or one domain: +66.7 versus +5.6 across models, 94.0% to 32.0% across domains. (7) Deltas of 1-3 points reported against standard errors of 0.8-1.4 from a single evolution run. The common factor is not a weak proposer; it is a signal that is shared between the thing being optimized and the thing being measured.

nodes.title: Mutation score's correlation with real-fault detection collapses once test-suite size is controlled
nodes.body: Papadakis, Yoo, Shin and Bae (ICSE 2018, pp.537-548, 'Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection?') recomputed the mutation-score / real-fault correlation on CoreBench and Defects4J while holding test-suite size fixed. All reported correlations become weak. The earlier strong result (Just et al., FSE 2014, pp.654-665) was a size confound: bigger suites both kill more mutants and detect more real faults, so the two move together without either measuring the other. Operational consequence for a grader: a mutation score is only interpretable conditional on suite size, and any loop that lets the graded agent add tests can raise the score by adding tests alone, with no change to fault-detection ability.
nodes.source: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8453121/ (ICSE 2018 pp.537-548); confounded prior: Just et al. FSE 2014 pp.654-665

nodes.title: Google's production mutation service reports a median of 7 mutants per changelist after filtering, and 89% of what it reports is judged useful
nodes.body: Google (arXiv:2102.11378, IEEE TSE 2022; ICSE-SEIP 2018 pp.163-171) runs mutation testing across ~2 billion LOC, >500,000,000 test executions/day, 60,000 changelists/day, 13,000 CIs, >24,000 developers and >1,000 projects, over 10 languages with 5 operators (AOR, LCR, ROR, UOI, SBR).
